Robert Bruce of Kinnaird
ROB-ert broos of kin-AIRD
proper noun
From the Scots surname Bruce, of Norman-French origin (de Brus), borne by the royal house of Scotland; the given name Robert is Germanic, “bright fame.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Robert Bruce (c. 1554–1631), laird of Kinnaird, forsook the prospect of earthly greatness to serve Christ in the ministry, succeeding John Knox in the pulpit of St. Giles at Edinburgh, where his preaching carried such weight that men said he was the most powerful preacher in Scotland since the great Reformer himself. His Sermons upon the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper remain a treasure of Reformed devotion, teaching that in the Supper we do not receive a new Christ but the same Christ more fully, that the sign and the thing signified are joined by the Spirit and not by any carnal presence in the elements. For his faithfulness Bruce was banished by King James, hounded from charge to charge, and confined for long years to Inverness, yet the LORD honoured his exile, and multitudes were converted under his northern ministry. A man of deep and often agonising communion, wrestling with assurance until it was given, he laboured that souls might close with Christ by faith. Called to the table of his Lord even at the hour of his death, he ate, blessed God, and said his Master called him. His life preaches that the true minister measures his greatness not by court favour but by faithfulness to the crown rights of the Redeemer, counting banishment for the gospel a lighter thing than silence.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Scottish Reformed preacher and successor of Knox at Edinburgh, famed for his sermons on the Lord’s Supper.

expand to see more

Robert Bruce of Kinnaird (c. 1554–1631), Scottish minister who left a noble inheritance for the gospel ministry.

Succeeded John Knox in the chief pulpit of Edinburgh and was reckoned among the mightiest preachers of the Scottish Kirk.

Author of the enduring Sermons upon the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper, a model of Reformed sacramental teaching.

Banished and long confined by King James for resisting royal encroachment upon the church’s liberties.

A man of profound spiritual conflict and assurance, whose northern exile bore abundant fruit in conversions.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of faithful preaching under persecution.

expand to see more

Robert Bruce is preserved not because his memory is disputed but because it is neglected. In an age that prizes ease and applause, the church has need of his example: a man who traded certain earthly honour for a persecuted pulpit, and who taught the Supper with a reverence and Christ-centredness that rebukes both the empty memorialism and the carnal sacramentalism of later times.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What must be recovered from Bruce is the principle of faithful, Spirit-anointed preaching that will not bend to the powers of the day. He held that Christ is truly given to faith in the Supper, that the minister answers to the King of the church and not to earthly kings, and that exile borne for the gospel is honour, not shame. His perseverance under banishment preaches to every believer that faithfulness, not comfort, is the measure of a life.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name gathers up the Scottish Reformation’s recovery of Word-centred preaching and a spiritual, Spirit-wrought view of the sacraments.

expand to see more

Rooted in Knox’s Reformation, Bruce inherited and preserved a preaching ministry that set the Word above all.

His sacramental theology follows Calvin: Christ received by faith through the Spirit, not by any change in the elements.

His sufferings prefigure the Covenanter witness that Christ alone is King and Head of His church.

His agonising over assurance mirrors the Puritan pursuit of a well-grounded confidence in Christ.

His northern exile shows the LORD turning the malice of kings into the ingathering of souls.

Usage

"Bruce’s Sermons on the Sacrament are cited whenever Reformed churches recover a high and spiritual view of the Lord’s table."

"His life is invoked as a pattern of ministerial faithfulness that prefers a banished pulpit to a silenced conscience."

"Historians of the Kirk name him the chief preacher of Edinburgh in the generation after Knox."
